title: Double-entry bookkeeping
examples: What is the basic rule for debit and credit?
How do I use a T-account to record a sale?
Does every transaction affect only one account?

explain.say: Today we are learning about double-entry bookkeeping. This system is fundamental to accounting.
The accounting equation must always balance. It states assets equal liabilities plus capital.
We use T-accounts to show these two effects. The debit side is on the left, and the credit side is on the right.
Debit increases assets and expenses. Credit increases liabilities and capital. This is the core rule.

draw.text: Debit increases A/E; Credit increases L/C

explain.say: For example, if you buy equipment using cash. Equipment, an asset, increases, so it is debited. Cash, also an asset, decreases, so it is credited.

draw.text: Buy Equipment: Debit Equipment, Credit Cash

explain.say: In real life, when you pay your electricity bill. Your expense increases, so you debit the expense account. Your bank account, an asset, decreases, so you credit it.

draw.text: Paying Bills: Debit Expense, Credit Bank

faq.q: Why do I have to use both debit and credit?
faq.a: Because every single financial event affects at least two different accounts. This ensures the accounting equation always balances out.
asks: What is the double entry concept?
Why is balancing important in accounting?

faq.q: Does debit always mean money is coming in?
faq.a: No, debit only means that account is on the left side of the T-account. It could be an expense going up, not just money coming in.
asks: Is debit always a positive amount?
What does the left side of the T-account show?

faq.q: If I receive cash, do I debit or credit?
faq.a: If you receive cash, your cash asset increases. Since assets increase with a debit, you will debit the cash account.
asks: When cash increases, what do I do?
Which side increases when I get money?

faq.q: What if I only record one side of a transaction?
faq.a: If you only record one side, your books will not balance, and your financial records will be incorrect. This is why double-entry is necessary.
asks: What happens if I forget the credit?
Can I only record the debit side?

faq.q: Are T-accounts just for practice or for real work?
faq.a: T-accounts are a simple tool to help you visualize the double-entry process. The final records go into the ledger.
asks: Are T-accounts the same as a ledger?
How do I move from T-accounts to the final report?

facts: Assets increase with a debit entry.
Liabilities and Capital increase with a credit entry.
Every transaction must have equal total debits and total credits.
A T-account visually separates the debit side from the credit side.

quiz.say: A business owner invests personal cash into the business. Which accounts are affected?
quiz.why: Capital represents the owner's investment, which increases with a credit, and cash, an asset, increases with a debit.

wrong.0: This records buying equipment, not the owner investing cash into the business.
wrong.2: You cannot debit capital because capital increases with a credit, not a debit.
wrong.3: This would show both assets and capital decreasing, which is incorrect for an investment.

quiz.say: A business pays rent for the month. Which entry correctly records this expense?
quiz.show: Rent Paid: Debit Rent Expense, Credit Cash
quiz.why: Expenses increase with a debit, and paying cash decreases the asset cash, which is credited.

wrong.0: This would imply that both the expense and the cash are somehow increasing or being credited.
wrong.2: This incorrectly suggests that receiving cash reduces your expense account.
wrong.3: You cannot debit both accounts because the total debits must equal the total credits.

quiz.say: If a business takes out a bank loan, what is the correct double entry?
quiz.show: Loan Taken: Debit Cash, Credit Loan Payable
quiz.why: Cash, an asset, increases with a debit. The loan payable, a liability, increases with a credit.

wrong.0: This would show both the asset and the liability decreasing, which is impossible when receiving a loan.
wrong.2: This suggests the loan liability is decreasing while cash is decreasing, which is wrong.
wrong.3: You cannot debit both accounts because the total debits must equal the total credits.
